title: The Cry in the Corridor
paragraphs: At first, every day that passed was exactly like the one before for Mary Lennox. Each morning she woke in her tapestried room and found Martha kneeling at the hearth, building the fire. Each morning she ate breakfast in the nursery, which had nothing in it to amuse her. After every breakfast she gazed out the window at the huge moor, which seemed to stretch out in every direction and climb right up to the sky. After staring for a while, she realized that if she did not go outside she would have to stay in and do nothing—so out she went. She did not know it was the best thing she could have done. She did not know that when she began to walk fast, or even run, along the paths and down the avenue, she was stirring up her slow blood. She was making herself stronger by struggling against the wind that swept down from the moor. She ran only to get warm, and she hated the wind that rushed at her face, roared, and held her back as if it were some giant she could not see. But the big breaths of rough, fresh air blowing over the heather filled her lungs with something good for her whole thin body. They whipped some red into her cheeks and brightened her dull eyes, and she had no idea it was happening.

But after a few days spent almost entirely outdoors, she woke one morning knowing what it was to be hungry. When she sat down to breakfast, she did not look scornfully at her porridge and push it away. She picked up her spoon, began to eat, and kept on eating until her bowl was empty.
“You did well with that this morning, didn’t you?” said Martha.
“It tastes good today,” said Mary, feeling a little surprised herself.

“It’s the air of the moor that’s giving you a stomach for your food,” answered Martha. “It’s lucky for you that you’ve got food as well as appetite. There’s been twelve in our cottage with the stomach for it and nothing to put in it. You keep on playing out of doors every day and you’ll get some flesh on your bones, and you won’t be so yellow.”
“I don’t play,” said Mary. “I have nothing to play with.”

“Nothing to play with!” exclaimed Martha. “Our children play with sticks and stones. They just run about and shout and look at things.” Mary did not shout, but she did look at things. There was nothing else to do. She walked round and round the gardens and wandered along the paths in the park. Sometimes she looked for Ben Weatherstaff. Though she saw him at work several times, he was either too busy to look at her or too grumpy. Once, when she was walking toward him, he picked up his spade and turned away, as if he did it on purpose.

There was one place she went to more often than any other. It was the long walk outside the gardens with the walls around them. There were bare flower beds on either side of it, and ivy grew thickly against the walls. In one spot, the creeping dark green leaves were bushier than anywhere else. It looked as if that part had been neglected for a long time. The rest of the ivy had been clipped and made neat, but at this lower end of the walk it had not been trimmed at all.

A few days after she had talked to Ben Weatherstaff, Mary stopped to notice this and wondered why it was so. She had just paused and was looking up at a long spray of ivy swinging in the wind when she saw a gleam of scarlet and heard a bright chirp. There on top of the wall sat Ben Weatherstaff’s robin redbreast, leaning forward to look at her with his small head tilted to one side.
“Oh!” she cried out. “Is it you? Is it you?” It did not seem at all strange to her that she spoke to him as if she were sure he would understand and answer.

And he did answer. He twittered and chirped and hopped along the wall as if he were telling her all sorts of things. It seemed to Mistress Mary that she understood him, too, even though he was not speaking in words. It was as if he said:
“Good morning! Isn’t the wind nice? Isn’t the sun nice? Isn’t everything nice? Let’s both chirp and hop and twitter. Come on! Come on!”
Mary began to laugh. As he hopped and took little flights along the wall, she ran after him. Poor little thin, sallow, ugly Mary—for a moment she actually looked almost pretty.

“I like you! I like you!” she cried, pattering down the walk. She chirped and tried to whistle, though she had no idea how to do that at all. But the robin seemed quite satisfied, and he chirped and whistled back at her. At last he spread his wings and darted up to the top of a tree, where he perched and sang loudly.

That reminded Mary of the first time she had seen him. He had been swinging on a treetop then, and she had been standing in the orchard. Now she was on the other side of the orchard, standing on the path outside a wall—much lower down—and there was the same tree inside.
“It’s in the garden no one can go into,” she said to herself. “It’s the garden without a door. He lives in there. How I wish I could see what it’s like!”

She ran up the walk to the green door she had come through the first morning. Then she ran down the path through the other door and into the orchard. When she stood and looked up, there was the tree on the other side of the wall, and there was the robin, just finishing his song and starting to preen his feathers with his beak.
“It is the garden,” she said. “I’m sure it is.”

She walked all the way around and looked closely at that side of the orchard wall, but she found only what she had found before—there was no door in it. Then she ran through the kitchen gardens again and out into the walk beside the long ivy-covered wall. She walked to the end of it and looked, but there was no door. Then she walked to the other end, looking again, and still there was no door.
“It’s very strange,” she said. “Ben Weatherstaff said there was no door, and there is no door. But there must have been one ten years ago, because Mr. Craven buried the key.”

This gave her so much to think about that she began to be quite interested, and she felt she was not sorry after all that she had come to Misselthwaite Manor. In India she had always felt too hot and too listless to care much about anything. The truth was that the fresh wind from the moor had begun to blow the cobwebs out of her young brain and wake her up a little.

She stayed outdoors nearly all day. When she sat down to supper that night, she felt hungry and drowsy and comfortable. She did not feel cross when Martha chattered away. She felt she rather liked hearing her, and at last she thought she would ask her a question. She asked it after she had finished supper and sat down on the hearth rug in front of the fire.
“Why did Mr. Craven hate the garden?” she said.

She had made Martha stay with her, and Martha had not minded at all. She was very young and used to a crowded cottage full of brothers and sisters. She found it dull in the great servants’ hall downstairs, where the footman and the upper housemaids made fun of her Yorkshire speech, looked down on her as a common little thing, and sat whispering among themselves. Martha liked to talk, and the strange child who had lived in India and been waited on by “blacks” was novelty enough to attract her.
She sat down on the hearth herself, without waiting to be asked.
“Are you still thinking about that garden?” she said. “I knew you would. That was just how it was with me when I first heard about it.”
“Why did he hate it?” Mary persisted.
Martha tucked her feet under her and made herself quite comfortable.
“Listen to the wind wuthering round the house,” she said. “You could hardly stand up on the moor if you were out on it tonight.”

Mary did not know what “wuthering” meant until she listened, and then she understood. It must mean that hollow, shuddering sort of roar that rushed round and round the house, as if the giant no one could see were pounding on it and beating at the walls and windows to break in. But you knew he could not get in, and somehow it made you feel very safe and warm inside a room with a red coal fire.
“But why did he hate it so?” she asked, after she had listened. She meant to find out, if Martha knew.
Then Martha gave up her store of knowledge.

“Mind,” she said, “Mrs. Medlock said it’s not to be talked about. There’s lots of things in this place that’s not to be talked over. That’s Mr. Craven’s orders. His troubles are none of the servants’ business, he says. But if it weren’t for the garden he wouldn’t be like he is. It was Mrs. Craven’s garden. She made it when they were first married, and she just loved it, and they used to tend the flowers themselves. And none of the gardeners was ever let in. He and she used to go in and shut the door and stay there hours and hours, reading and talking. And she was just a bit of a girl, and there was an old tree with a branch bent like a seat on it. She made roses grow over it, and she used to sit there. But one day when she was sitting there, the branch broke and she fell to the ground and was hurt so badly that she died the next day. The doctors thought he’d go out of his mind and die, too. That’s why he hates it. No one’s ever gone in since, and he won’t let anyone talk about it.”
Mary did not ask any more questions. She looked at the red fire and listened to the wind “wuthering.” It seemed to be “wuthering” louder than ever.

At that moment, something very good was happening to her. In fact, four good things had happened to her since she came to Misselthwaite Manor. She had felt as if she understood a robin and he understood her. She had run in the wind until her blood grew warm. She had been healthily hungry for the first time in her life. And she had found out what it was to feel sorry for someone.

But as she listened to the wind, she began to listen to something else. She did not know what it was, because at first she could hardly tell it apart from the wind itself. It was a strange sound—it seemed almost as if a child were crying somewhere. Sometimes the wind sounded a good deal like a child crying, but soon Mistress Mary felt quite sure this sound was inside the house, not outside it. It was far away, but it was inside. She turned around and looked at Martha.
“Do you hear someone crying?” she said.
Martha suddenly looked confused.
“No,” she answered. “It’s the wind. Sometimes it sounds like someone’s lost on the moor and wailing. It’s got all sorts of sounds.”
“But listen,” said Mary. “It’s in the house—down one of those long corridors.”

And at that very moment a door must have been opened somewhere downstairs, because a great rushing draft blew along the passage. The door of the room where they sat was blown open with a crash. They both jumped to their feet, and the light went out. The crying sound was swept down the far corridor, so that it could be heard more plainly than ever.
“There!” said Mary. “I told you so! It is someone crying—and it isn’t a grown-up.”

Martha ran and shut the door and turned the key. But before she did, they both heard a door in some far passage shut with a bang, and then everything was quiet, because even the wind stopped “wuthering” for a few moments.
“It was the wind,” said Martha stubbornly. “And if it wasn’t, it was little Betty Butterworth, the scullery maid. She’s had the toothache all day.”
But something troubled and awkward in her manner made Mistress Mary stare hard at her. She did not believe Martha was telling the truth.
